content: The sebaceous glands are specialized glands located in the skin of mammals. These glands are classified as a branched type of acinar gland and are distributed throughout human skin, except on the palms of the hands and soles of the feet. They are most commonly found in areas covered by hair, where they are connected to hair follicles. Sebaceous glands secrete an oily substance called sebum onto the hair, which is then transported to the skin surface along the hair shaft. The combined structure of the hair, hair follicle, arrector pili muscle, and sebaceous gland is referred to as a pilosebaceous unit. Sebaceous glands are also present in non-hair-bearing areas of the skin, such as the eyelids, penis, labia minora, and nipples. In these regions, sebum is delivered to the skin surface through ducts that terminate in sweat pores. A specialized form of sebaceous gland, known as the meibomian gland, is located at the rim of the eyelids. These glands secrete sebum into the tear film that coats the eye, helping to slow the evaporation of tears. Sebum, the oily substance secreted by sebaceous glands, is composed of lipids and the remnants of dead fat-producing cells. Sebum is produced within specialized cells in the gland and is released when these cells rupture, classifying sebaceous glands as holocrine glands. While sebum itself is odorless, its breakdown by bacteria can produce odors. Sebum plays a role in protecting and waterproofing the hair and skin, preventing them from becoming dry, brittle, or cracked. It also inhibits the growth of microorganisms on the skin. Excess sebum production can lead to an oily appearance of the skin and hair, particularly if not washed regularly. Sebum is also a component of earwax. The composition of sebum varies across species. In humans, its lipid content includes a variety of fatty acids, wax esters, and other lipids. During fetal development, sebaceous glands secrete a substance called vernix caseosa, a waxy or cheesy white coating that covers the skin of newborns. Sebaceous gland activity increases during puberty due to elevated androgen levels. In males, sebaceous glands become more prominent on the penis during and after puberty, which is a normal physiological change and should not be mistaken for a sexually transmitted disease. In females, these glands are more prominent in the labia minora. Sebaceous glands are implicated in several skin conditions, including acne and keratosis pilaris. The prescription medication isotretinoin significantly reduces sebum production and is commonly used to treat acne. Excessive use of anabolic steroids, often by bodybuilders, can overstimulate sebaceous glands, leading to acne. Blockage of a sebaceous gland can result in a sebaceous cyst. Enlarged sebaceous glands can lead to a condition known as sebaceous hyperplasia, while seborrheic dermatitis is another common condition involving these glands. Sebaceous gland carcinoma is a rare and aggressive cancer of the sebaceous glands, whereas sebaceous adenoma is a benign tumor of these glands. In other animals, sebaceous glands serve additional functions. Certain species of Demodex mites feed on sebum and are commonly found in the sebaceous glands of mammals, including humans. In rodents such as mice and rats, the preputial glands are large modified sebaceous glands that produce pheromones.
